reception.text: The May 9, 1904 order went out on the wire and ran nationally the next morning; the San Diego Union and Daily Bee printed all seven instructions on page one under the headline "NO GAMBLING ON THE STRIP."
reception.source: San Diego Union and Daily Bee, May 10, 1904, p. 1

reception.text: Papers in Los Angeles, San Francisco, Fresno and Denver, and Colorado weeklies within the week, reported that Davis would be governor and the Commission would make the Zone's laws.
reception.source: Los Angeles Herald, May 10, 1904; Rocky Mountain News, May 10, 1904; Golden Weekly Globe, May 14, 1904

reception.text: Democrats, anti-imperialists and parts of the press charged that the United States had helped Panama break from Colombia and taken the Isthmus by something close to force; the governing machinery itself drew little controversy.

political_impact.text: Governor George W. Davis reached Colón on May 17, 1904, was received by President Amador on May 19, and that day published his announcement to the inhabitants of the Zone.
The Commission's power to make the Zone's laws was a temporary grant that ran to the end of the Fifty-eighth Congress and was later extended.

Roosevelt's libel prosecution of the New York World and Indianapolis News over the $40,000,000 canal-company payment failed; the Supreme Court ruled the federal law used did not reach the conduct and never decided whether the articles were libelous.
political_impact.source: United States v. Press Publishing Co., 219 U.S. 1 (1911)

political_impact.text: Colombia protested the loss of its province and pressed its claims for nearly twenty years; the Reyes mission's arbitration proposal was rejected in January 1904, and Colombia declined to ratify the Root–Cortés treaties of 1909.

At Berkeley on March 23, 1911, Roosevelt said, "Accordingly I took the Isthmus, started the canal, and then left Congress — not to debate the canal, but to debate me." Colombia's minister protested the remark to Secretary Knox.
political_impact.source: University of California Chronicle, vol. XIII, no. 2 (April 1911), p. 139

legacy.text: The Commission built the Panama Canal, which opened to traffic when the SS Ancon made the first official transit; the formal opening was proclaimed July 12, 1920.
The Canal Zone ceased to exist as a jurisdiction when the Torrijos–Carter Treaties took effect.
The canal itself passed to Panama.
The Thomson–Urrutia Treaty, proclaimed in 1922 with its apology article removed, paid Colombia $25,000,000 in installments through 1926; Colombia called it an indemnity and the treaty said otherwise.
legacy.source: Thomson–Urrutia Treaty; FRUS 1919, vol. I, doc. 727

today.name: Panama Canal Zone
today.note: The executive-branch government organized in 1904 ran the Zone until it ceased to exist as a jurisdiction on October 1, 1979.
